extracted.intended_audience: editors, authors, copyeditors, and publishers (academic and professional)
extracted.subtask_description: A publishing style manual (University of Chicago Press) covering capitalization, use of small caps, italics, quotations, spelling, and punctuation — rules for preparing manuscripts and official printed matter. Includes many field-specific exceptions and typographic/formatting guidance with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of species names (botanical/zoological vs geological/medical)
rubrics_metrics.description: In botanical and zoological matter, the names of species, if derived from names of persons or from generic names, are to be capitalized; in geological and medical matter the names of species are never capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felis leo, Cocos nucifera, Rosa Carolina, Parkinsonia Torreyana, Styrax californica, Lythrum hyssopifolia, Phyteuma Halleri, Carex Halleriana; but (geological) Pterygomatopus schmidti, Conodectus Javosus. (See also rule 71.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes should be capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kafir, Negro, Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese, Celestials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize astronomical solar-system body names (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In astronomical work, capitalize the names of bodies of our solar system except 'sun,' 'earth,' 'moon,' and 'stars'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Milky Way, the Great Bear, Saturn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize official university divisions/offices/courses in official work
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University (or similar institutions) are capitalized in official work when used as official names; generic references are lowercased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the University, the School of Education (but: the school), the University Extension Division (but: the division), the Department of Anthropology (but: the department); the Board of Trustees, the Trustees, the Board; the Senate; the Faculty of the College of Commerce and Administration (but: the faculty); President, Registrar, Professor of Physics, Assistant in Chemistry, Fellow, Scholar. Also guidance on formatting addresses and signature lines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use capitals and small capitals for date/location lines and salutatory phrases in letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of town and state in the date line, the salutatory phrase at the beginning of letters, and the signature and residence at the end of letters/articles should be set in capitals and small capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formatting: set date line to the right with one em indent, preferably in smaller type than the body; salutatory line (e.g., 'My dear Mr. Smith:') set flush with a colon on a separate line. Examples: Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1911; Charles W. Scott (signature line formatting guidance provided). Centered address lines in small caps for multi-line addresses; date centered and in caps and lower case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal-document lead words (Whereas, Note, Section) capitalization and abbreviation
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions use 'Whereas'; in notes (not footnotes) use 'Note.' followed by a period and a dash; in constitutions/by-laws use 'Section' introducing paragraphs followed by a number and generally abbreviate 'Sec.' after the first occurrence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Note. — It should be noticed that .... ; Section 1. This association shall be styled .... ; usual practice: Section 1. ... Sec. 2. ...

rubrics_metrics.name: Set a.m., p.m., B.C., A.D. in small capitals without spaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviations ante/post meridiem and B.C./A.D. should be set in small capitals and printed without a space between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C., 1906 A.D. (See related rules 22, 103, 106.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowercase commonized proper names and derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Words of common usage originally proper names and their derivatives, and generally verbs derived from proper names, should begin with a small (lower-case) initial letter when the origin is obscured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, bonanza, china, morocco, guinea-pig, boycott, roman (type), italicize, christianize, anglicize, macadamize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowercase minor subdivisions and their abbreviations in literary references
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor subdivisions (chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note) and their abbreviations (chap., sec., p., art., vs., l., n.) are given in lower case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 37, 110, and 237 for cross-references; use consistent abbreviation forms in bibliographic contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small initial letter for units of measurement abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Units of measurement and their abbreviations are written with small (lower-case) initials when used in normal text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: h. = hour, min. = minute, sec. = second; lb. = pound, oz. = ounce; yd. = yard, ft. = foot; etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italic side-heads: capitalize first word and proper names only
rubrics_metrics.description: In italic side-heads (side headings set in italics), capitalize only the first word and any proper names; other words should be lower-case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rules 172 and 280 for further guidance and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize the first word of a quotation connected to preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: When a quotation is run into the text and is immediately connected with what precedes, the first word of that quotation is capitalized even if it begins a sentence in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See illustrations and exceptions in rules 35 and 131.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize words or phrases for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics to lend emphasis or importance to words or phrases in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This was, however, not the case'; 'It is sufficiently plain that the sciences of life, at least, are studies of processes.' Use sparingly for emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize foreign words/phrases not incorporated into English, with exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Words and phrases from foreign languages inserted into English text and not assimilated into English should be italicized; single sentences or brief passages in a foreign language should generally be italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung', 'Napoleon's coup d'etat', 'De gustibus non est disputandum'. Do not italicize foreign titles preceding names, names of foreign institutions/places with established English usage (Pere Lagrange, Freiherr von Schwenau; the German Reichstag), nor words that have become anglicized (ennui, cafe, resume, naive, debris). See long list of examples in rule 59/60.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize titles of publications (books, pamphlets, periodicals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of books (including plays, essays, cycles of poems, and substantial single poems), pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, periodicals, proceedings, and transactions should be set in italics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer Night's Dream; the Independent; the Chicago Tribune; Transactions of the Illinois Society for Child Study. Note exceptions for lengthy bibliographies or tables and footnote practices of some journals (e.g., Botanical Gazette). Books of the Bible and ancient manuscript titles are set in roman (see rules 31 and 44).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize certain Latin/legal bibliographic abbreviations; do not italicize others
rubrics_metrics.description: Words/phrases and abbreviations used in literary and legal references such as ad loc, circa (ca.), et al., ibid., idem, infra, loc. cit., op. cit., passim, sic, supra, s.v., vide, should be italicized; but cf., e.g., i.e., V. (versus), viz., etc. should not be italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply italicization selectively for commonly italicized Latin terms in scholarly apparatus; avoid italics for frequent abbreviations like cf., e.g., i.e.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize 'See' and 'See also' in indexes and 'for'/'read' in errata
rubrics_metrics.description: In an index or similar compilation, use italics for 'See' and 'See also' when differentiation is desirable; use italics for the words 'for' and 'read' in errata lists to separate incorrect and correct readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: See also Sociology; for levee read levee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize names of plaintiff/defendant in legal citations and proceedings' titles
rubrics_metrics.description: In legal citations italicize the names of plaintiff and defendant and the titles of proceedings containing prefixes such as in re, ex parte, In the matter of, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Conolly v. Union Sewer Pipe Co.; In re Smith; Ex parte Brown; In the matter of the petition of Henry Robinson for a writ of habeas corpus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and capitalize address lines in speeches and primary letter address lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Address lines in speeches, reports, and primary address lines in letters should be set flush, on a separate line, with nouns capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen:'; 'Mr. John Smith, 321 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill.'; 'Dear Sir: I take pleasure in announcing ....' (See rule 64.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature titles: formatting and capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: In signatures, the position or title added after the name is formatted depending on length: one-word titles run into same line; multi-word titles centered under name with indention rules; very long titles centered and set flush on second line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Arthur P. Maguire, Secretary; Yours very truly, Carter H. Harrison, Mayor of Chicago; Charles M. Gayley, Professor of English Language and Literature. Subject to special-case exigencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a), b), c) and a, b, c affixed to numbers for subdivisions and fractional parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parenthetical a), b), c), etc. to indicate subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph, double when run in); use a, b, c affixed to numbers of verse, page, etc., to denote fractional parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example usage: Luke 4:31a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use letters to designate unknown quantities and lines in technical/mathematical matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters are used to designate unknown quantities, lines, or powers in algebraic, geometrical, and similar matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ac + bc = c(a + b); the lines od and y1/2; the nth power. Follow typographic conventions for mathematical letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use letters in legends referring to illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters used in legends or in the text that refer to corresponding letters in accompanying illustrations should be set appropriately (usually italic or roman per context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'At the point A above (see diagram).'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to particular letters (naming letters) formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to particular letters, use phrasing like 'the letter u, a small v.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear typographic distinction between referencing a letter-as-letter and using the letter in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use abbreviations for older currency units following numerals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use abbreviations like s. and d. (shillings and pence) following numerals when indicating such amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 35s. 6d. (See cross-reference 270.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize scientific (Latin) names of genera and species in zoological/botanical/geological/paleontological contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific Latin names of genera and species when used together (generic in nominative singular) should be italicized in zoological, geological, and paleontological matter; in botanical, geological, and paleontological matter names of genera and species when used together, and genera when used alone, also italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felis leo, Rosa Carolina, Conodecies favosiss, Phyteuma Halteri; Acer saccharum, Basidiobolus, Alternaria, Erythrosuchus. Exception: in medical matter the general practice is to print such names in roman, avoiding italics altogether. See also astronomical exceptions below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical names and catalog designations typographic rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In astronomical/astrophysical matter: (a) Greek, Latin, and Arabic names of planets, satellites, constellations, and individual stars are treated (examples given); (b) designations from well-known catalogues, Flamsteed numbers, Baeyer letters use roman catalogue notation; (c) chemical element symbols are set (see punctuation rule 123); (d) certain Fraunhofer line letters are lower-case and italicization varies — spectral type letters are not italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jupiter, Tethys, Lyra, Antares, ip Orionis (but: Orion-type stars); M13 (Messier); Bond 619; N.G.C. 6165; 85 Pegasi; H, Ca, Ti (element symbols); Fraunhofer lines: o, b, g, h (lower-case)—but not capital letters A–H and K; spectral types As, B3, Mb are not italicized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Resolved.' in resolutions formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions set the word 'Resolved.' (capitalized) to introduce resolved clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference rule 39; typographic convention in formal resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Continued' after headlines/titles and 'To be continued' at article ends
rubrics_metrics.description: After headlines or titles, as a rule, use the word 'Continued' and place 'To be continued' at the end of articles that will continue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example headline formatting: THE SCOPE OF SOCIOLOGY— Continued; end-of-article note: [To be continued]. See rule 179 for extended guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations: run-into-text citations use quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations of a passage from an author that are run into the text should be enclosed in quotation marks (roman type for quotes run into text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 85 for long quotation formatting; example: short inline citation within text should have quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotations from different authors or works placed consecutively should be quoted
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotations from different authors, or different works by the same author, following each other uninterrupted by original matter (or by references other than footnote markers) should each be placed between quotation marks even if reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 85-87 for handling reduced citations and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Words/phrases accompanied by definitions should be in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: A word or phrase that is immediately followed by its definition should be enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Drop-folio' means a page-number at the foot of the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusual, technical, or ironical words/phrases should be quoted
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for unusual, technical, ironical, or attention-directing words or phrases in the text, even if accompanied by qualifiers like 'so-called.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Her 'five o'clocks' were famous; She was wearing a gown of 'lobster-colored' silk; This so-called 'man of affairs'.

rubrics_metrics.name: In translations, give the English equivalent in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: When translating, present the English equivalent of a foreign word or phrase in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weltanschauung, 'world-view' or 'fundamental aspect of life'; Mommsen Romische Geschichte ('History of Rome').

rubrics_metrics.name: Use quotation marks to indicate the particular word(s) to which attention is directed
rubrics_metrics.description: When directing attention to a specific term, enclose that term in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the term 'lynch law'; the phrase 'liberty of conscience'; the concepts 'good' and 'bad'; the name 'Chicago'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serial titles should be enclosed in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of series or serials should be set in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'English Men of Letters' series; 'International Critical Commentary'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of shorter poems should be in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of shorter poems should be enclosed in quotation marks rather than italicized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Shelley's 'To a Skylark.' (See rule 60 for longer works.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cited titles of subdivisions and shorter works in quotes; major divisions capitalized without quotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Cited titles of subdivisions (parts, books, chapters), titles of papers, lectures, sermons, articles, toasts, mottoes, etc., should be in quotation marks. References to Preface, Introduction, Table of Contents, Index, etc., of a specific work should be capitalized without quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. I, 'The British School,' chap. ii, 'John Stuart Mill'; The subject of the lecture was 'Japan — Its Past, Present, and Future'; Preface, p. iii (no quotes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of ships in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of ships should be set in quotation marks, often with the ship's prefix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the U.S. SS. 'Oregon'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of pictures and works of art in quotation marks
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of pictures and works of art are enclosed in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Murillo's 'The Holy Family'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set long prose and poetry extracts in smaller type
rubrics_metrics.description: Prose extracts ordinarily making five or more lines in smaller type, and poetry citations of two lines or more, should be set in smaller type (reduced) rather than run into the main text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An isolated short prose quotation may be run into the text if organically related; short lines adjacent to longer reduced extracts may be reduced for uniform appearance. See rule 86 for size reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Size reduction recommendations for reduced citations
rubrics_metrics.description: General point-size reduction guidance: reduce from 11-pt and 10-pt to 9-pt; from 9-pt to 8-pt; from 8-pt to 6-pt, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See rule 252 for additional technical type-setting guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced citations should not use quotation marks (usually)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduced citations (block quotations) should not have quotation marks, and, as a rule, quotation marks should not be used with italics in reduced citations except in special cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions as noted in rule 75 and elsewhere; follow consistency for block quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks should include ellipses and 'etc.' when they indicate omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should always include ellipses and the phrase 'etc.' when necessary to show that part of the quotation is omitted, taking care to maintain perfect clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples to show when 'etc.' stands for omitted material in the quoted matter and when it stands outside the quotation to show a broader omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat opening quotation marks for each paragraph of a broken quotation
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoted prose is broken into paragraphs, repeat the opening quotation marks at the beginning of each paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves the visible scope of the quotation across paragraph breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear (project) quotation marks when alignment is desired
rubrics_metrics.description: If alignment of quotation lines is desired, quotation marks should be 'cleared' so they project beyond the line of alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided in rule 90 showing opening quote projecting to align text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use double quotation marks for primary quotations and single for nested quotations (alternate thereafter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Double quotation marks are used for primary quotations; for a quotation within a quotation use single marks; alternate back to double for a third nesting, single for a fourth, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The orator then proceeded: 'The dictionary tells us that

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out civil/military titles preceding names (with listed exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: All civil and military titles and forms of address preceding a name should be spelled out except for the abbreviations Mr., Messrs., Mrs., Dr., Rev., Hon.; 'Esq.' following the name should be abbreviated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use 'General Schofield' spelled out; do not, except in quotations, set 'the Rev.,' 'the Hon.'; abbreviate Esquire as 'Esq.' following the name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out Christian names in ordinary reading-matter; treat 'von' as part of name
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian given names should be spelled out (George, Charles, John) rather than abbreviated except in quoted matter or original signatures; 'von' remains part of a person's name and is not abbreviated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use Geo., Chas., Jno. except in cited or quoted forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out numbers under three digits in ordinary reading-matter (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading-matter spell out all numbers of less than three digits (i.e., below 100) unless they are statistical/technical, or occur in groups of six or more in close succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'There are thirty-eight cities...' but use figures for technical/statistical contexts: 10°, 45 miles, 3 cubic feet, 24 pages, 100 bushels, 9 per cent, 45 pounds, $1,000. Treat connected groups consistently and if the largest contains three or more digits use figures for all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out round numbers where approximate
rubrics_metrics.description: Round (approximate) numbers should be spelled out (with guidance about levels of approximation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the attendance was estimated at five hundred' (but 'at 550'); 'a thesis of about three thousand words' (but 'of about 2,700'); write 'fifteen hundred' rather than 'one thousand five hundred' if chosen to spell out 1,500.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out numbers that begin sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers, regardless of size, that commence a sentence in ordinary reading-matter should be spelled out; when impracticable, reconstruct the sentence to avoid starting with a numeral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Five hundred and ninety-three men, 417 women, and 126 children...' or recast to 'The total number of those who went down with the ship was 593 men...'

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out isolated sums of money in ordinary reading-matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Sums of money occurring in isolated instances in ordinary text should be spelled out; when several monetary figures occur close together or in statistical treatment, use figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The admission was two dollars.' vs a list: 'Admission: men, $2; women, $1; children, 25 cents.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-of-day spelling conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Time of day is spelled out in ordinary reading matter ('at four', 'at half-past two in the afternoon', 'at seven o'clock'); statistically, in enumerations, and when used with A.M./P.M., use figures (4:15 P.M.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omit 'o'clock' when using figures with A.M./P.M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ages spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: Ages should be written out in words in ordinary text (eighty years and four months old; children between six and fourteen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow normal numeric rules for statistical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out numbers of centuries, dynasties, sessions, and similar entities
rubrics_metrics.description: Numbers of centuries, Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, military/regimental numbers, political divisions, and thoroughfares should be spelled out (unless brevity demands figures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nineteenth century; Fifth Dynasty; Fifty-fourth Congress, Second Session; Fifteenth Infantry; Sixth Congressional District; Fifth Avenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refer to particular decades in lower-case
rubrics_metrics.description: References to decades are given in lower-case (e.g., 'in the nineties').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use idiomatic lower-case phrasing rather than numeric decades in ordinary prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of months spelled out except in statistical/long lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Names of months should be spelled out in ordinary text, except in statistical matter or long enumerations where abbreviated or numeric month forms may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'from January 1 to April 15' (omit st, d, th after dates in normal prose).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'United States' capitalization exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: 'United States' is generally spelled out (capitalized) except in quotations and certain constructions (e.g., military suffixes General Schofield, U.S.A.; ship prefixes; in footnotes and similar references where U.S. or U.S. SS. may be used).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See cross-references 22, 52, 103 for contextual rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize 'Railroad/-way' and 'Fort/Mount/Port' in geographical names
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'Railroad' (or -way), and 'Fort', 'Mount', and 'Port' in geographical appellations are capitalized when part of proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad (avoid R.R. or Ry. in such contexts); Fort Wayne, Port Huron, Mount Elias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of publications usually spelled out; apply discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases, fully spell out names of publications. This rule is open to modification for particular instances; consider expediency, context, authoritative usage, and author's preference. If in doubt, spell out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors/editors advised to prefer spelling out names; good taste often forgives spelling-out errors more readily than the opposite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations for state names after towns (specified list)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a state, territory, or possession follows the name of a town, use the specified abbreviations without spaces between letters (list provided, e.g., Ala., Ariz., Cal., Conn., D.C., etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the provided list for consistent postal/typographic abbreviations; see cross-references 22, 52, 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ampersand and abbreviations for firm names in technical bibliographic matter; spell out in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matter (footnotes, bibliographies) use abbreviations like 'Co.' and ampersands in firm names (The Macmillan Co., Macmillan & Co.), while in normal text 'Company' and 'Brothers' may be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Macmillan Co., Harper Bros.; in text: 'Harper Brothers have recently published...'. Use editorial judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Saint' usage and Biblical book/versions abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Saint' is abbreviated as 'St.' before names (St. Louis), but often omitted before apostles, evangelists, and church fathers (Luke, Paul, Augustine); provide standard abbreviations for books of the Bible and common version abbreviations (A.V., R.V., A.R.V., LXX, Vulg., etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use provided standard abbreviation forms for Scripture and Apocrypha; follow the table for consistent citation (e.g., Gen., Exod., Lev., Matt., Mark, Luke, John, Acts, Rom., etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric and common measurement symbol practices in bibliographic contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow the common designations of weights and measures in the metric system and other symbols when following numerals (1 m., 2 dm., 3 cm., 4 mm.; cm. = cubic meter notation etc.) and use the list of common measurement symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cm., c.c., gm., gr., h., min., sec., lb., oz., yd., ft., in.; A.U. (Angstrom units), H.P. (horse-power), C. (centigrade), F. (Fahrenheit). See also rule 123 for punctuation of symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial rule for extracts' spelling/punctuation vs original when minor differences occur
rubrics_metrics.description: In extracts from modern authors whose spelling and punctuation differ slightly from current usage, adopt office (house) style where differences do not affect meaning; in Old English or where fidelity is essential follow the original. Titles must always be accurately quoted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use editorial judgment to modernize minor orthographic differences but preserve essential original forms when required by scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form possessive of proper names ending in s or sibilant
rubrics_metrics.description: For monosyllabic proper names ending in s or another sibilant form the possessive by adding 's; for names of more than one syllable add an apostrophe alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King James's Version, Burns's poems, Marx's theories; Moses' law, Jesus' birth, Demosthenes' orations, Berlioz' compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'a' before sounded h, long u, and the word 'one'
rubrics_metrics.description: Before a sounded 'h', long 'u', and before the word 'one' use the indefinite article 'a' rather than 'an'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a hotel, a harmonic, a historical, a union, a euphonious word, such a one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ligature use in quotations from Latin and anglicized derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use the ligature 'œ' and 'ae' separation in quotations from Latin or anglicized derivatives where e has not been substituted; retain ligature in Old English quotations and in modern French/other languages where correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Aurea prima sata est ... (separate letters in Latin); MUred, AS hwcete = 'w'heat' — in Old English retain ligature when appropriate; in French CEuvres de Balzac retain ligature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate 'farther' (distance) and 'further' (moreover)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'farther' to indicate physical distance or remoteness and 'further' to mean 'moreover' or 'in addition'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the farther end'; 'he went still farther'; 'further, he suggested'; 'a further reason'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'O' (vocative) without comma; use 'Oh,' with comma for exclamation
rubrics_metrics.description: In vocative forms use 'O' without a following comma; for exclamations use 'Oh,' followed by a comma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'O thou most mighty ruler!' vs 'Oh, why did not Cerberus drag me back to hell?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Participles retaining or omitting final 'e' — spelling guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain participles retain the final 'e' in the primary word (agreeing, hieing, singeing, dyeing, hoeing, tingeing, eyeing, shoeing, vieing); others omit the 'e' (acknowledging, gluing, judging, awing, grudging, owing, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific lists to follow editorial spelling conventions for -ing forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred American spellings list (extensive)
rubrics_metrics.description: A long list of preferred American spellings is provided (e.g., abridgment, center, favor, acknowledge vs British forms) and numerous specific word-pairs and variants are enumerated for house style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the supplied list as authoritative for house orthography; includes advice like: make one word of 'today', 'tomorrow', 'tonight', 'cannot'; distinguish 'sometimes' vs 'some time(s)'. See rule 119 for extensive examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate -ise and -ize terminations (which to use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prescribe which verbs/terminations are to be spelled -ise and which as -ize (with -yze variants where listed); detailed lists of verbs under each termination are provided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell 'advertise, comprise, enterprise, premise' with -ise; spell 'analyze, baptize, civilize, energize' with -ize. Use the lists to resolve variants like apprise/apprize and apprize (to appraise) vs apprise (to inform).

rubrics_metrics.name: All punctuation marks printed in the same style/font as the preceding word or letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Punctuation marks should be printed in the same style or font of type as the word or letter immediately preceding them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'With the cry of Banzai! the regiment stormed the hill'; Luke 4:16; No. 1. Ensure font consistency for punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period usage — end of complete sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a period to indicate the end of a complete sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See also related rules for abbreviations and ellipses (rule 125 cross-reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Periods after abbreviations (general rule and exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put a period after all abbreviations, except where mechanical necessity compels omission of a letter or letters in the middle of a word for which there is no recognized abbreviated form; treat metric symbols as abbreviations (with periods) but not chemical symbols nor the phrase 'per cent' nor book-format abbreviations like 4to, 8vo.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Macmillan & Co., Mr. Smith, St. Paul, No. 1, Chas. (see 93), ibid., s.v.; 10 mm.; but: m'f'g pl't (= manufacturing plant); O, Fe; 2 per cent; 4to, 8vo. Note exceptions for some journals: Astrophysical Journal may print '12 mm' without period (but 2° 3' 4" uses different spacing). Avoid periods on chemical symbols; treat metric symbols per journal house rules.
